glm.reason: Measures skill(∞) and curvature via a+b/M fits on subsamples instead of re-measuring skill at large M; compute buys asymptote estimates.

glm.quote: Make the unit of work one date. At fixed budget of ~7,000 fifteen-day forecasts, search the (dates × members) grid and pick the allocation that minimizes the standard error of the quantity of interest — skill gain past 50 members — instead of maximizing members per date.
glm.reason: Reorders compute across the dates×members grid; extra compute now buys date-variance reduction it previously could not, instead of saturating members.

glm.quote: Change the objective: measure the cap directly as tail calibration of the exchangeable distribution plus tail-error dependence.
glm.reason: Measures the cap directly (tail calibration, correlation ρ, N_eff) rather than the flattening symptom; compute buys new diagnostics, even recalibration.

reframes.bottleneck: Skill differences between member counts are averaged over only 7 held-fixed verification dates; across-date variance dominates the standard error of the skill-vs-N slope, so members past roughly 50-100 per date buy precision on a quantity that stays swamped by date noise. Extra members purchase more of the same.
reframes.assumption: That members per forecast is the compute axis that limits the answer, with the 7 verification dates held fixed.
reframes.reframe: Treat the run budget as an experimental-design problem: estimate the variance components (across-date vs within-date sampling) and reallocate a fixed number of member-forecasts across (dates x members) to minimize the standard error of the slope of skill vs log N, rather than maximizing members on few dates.
reframes.question: For a fixed budget of 3,000 member-forecasts, which (dates x members) allocation - 7x400, 15x200, or 30x100 - gives the smallest standard error on the slope of top-1% fair-Brier skill vs log2 N, measured against ERA5?
reframes.measure: Pilot: run 2 new dates at 200 members plus reuse the 50-member control (about 400 new runs, roughly $55, about 4 machine-hours). Estimate across-date and sampling variance of the Brier score at N=50 and N=200, then solve the analytic optimal-allocation formula for the fixed budget.
reframes.compute_after: The full budget buys the optimal split (likely around 30 dates x 100 members, roughly $413): extra compute then buys independent verification dates, i.e. new information, instead of redundant draws from one distribution.
reframes.exact: Standard error of the fitted slope of fair-Brier skill vs log2(members) for top-1% wind, temperature, and rain exceedance probabilities verified against ERA5.
reframes.expected: Across-date variance dominates at N>=50, so the optimal allocation shifts compute toward dates and the slope's standard error drops by roughly a factor of 2 at equal dollar cost.
reframes.fails_if: Within-date sampling variance still dominates at N=200, meaning large member counts genuinely add measurable skill and the original 1,000-member design stands.
reframes.closest_prior: HENS Part 2 [s_hens] ran 92 dates x 7,424 members but never reported the variance components or an optimal (dates x members) split; the afCRPS paper [s_crps_paper] used a fixed 51-member operational set.

reframes.bottleneck: Members are exchangeable draws of one afCRPS-trained distribution, so the N-dependence of any threshold-probability score is binomial sampling noise with a known 1/N form; running 1,000 members mostly measures arithmetic and cannot move the N-infinity cap set by model error.
reframes.assumption: That the saturation point and the asymptotic skill must be found empirically by actually running the large ensembles.
reframes.reframe: Change what is measured: fit the score's a + b/N law from nested subsamples of a few hundred members and extrapolate the N-infinity asymptote directly, instead of buying the curve point by point with full-fidelity members.
reframes.question: From a + b/N fits to fair-CRPS and fair-Brier on nested subsamples of 10-200 members over the 7 dates, is the extrapolated N-infinity skill for top-1% wind/temperature/rain probabilities statistically distinguishable from the N=50 skill (difference greater than 0.02 Brier)?
reframes.measure: Run 7 dates x 200 members (1,400 runs, roughly $193, about 15 machine-hours), or first test the 1/N law for free on the published 51-member ECMWF open-data control (about $0). Bootstrap subsample 10-200 members and fit per variable.
reframes.compute_after: If the asymptote is flat, the question is answered with about 5x less member compute, and the saved budget redirects to more dates or perturbed-model diversity; only a failed 1/N fit justifies the 1,000-member runs.
reframes.exact: Extrapolated N-infinity fair-Brier and fair-CRPS (the a parameter of the a + b/N fit) for top-1% wind/temperature/rain exceedance probabilities, with bootstrap confidence intervals.
reframes.expected: The 1/N law fits within bootstrap error and the asymptote lies within about 0.01 Brier of the N=50 value, demonstrating saturation from 200 members instead of 1,000.
reframes.fails_if: Scores deviate systematically from a + b/N (for example in the far tail, where member exchangeability could break down), meaning large-N runs carry real information and must be executed.
reframes.closest_prior: HENS [s_hens] demonstrated 4-sigma tail sampling at 7,424 members but did not test whether skill follows the exchangeable-draw a + b/N asymptote; standard Monte Carlo theory predicts it must if members are exchangeable.

reframes.bottleneck: The fixed 7-dates x 6-member-levels factorial commits all 7,000 runs before any data are examined; compute is spent even where the answer is already decided, while the real objective is binary - does skill keep rising past 50 members, yes or no - not the full curve.
reframes.assumption: That the experiment needs a fixed design at six member levels, fully executed before analysis begins.
reframes.reframe: Change the objective to the yes/no decision and reorder the work: a group-sequential test that adds members in batches of 50 and stops as soon as the confidence interval on the skill gain versus the 50-member baseline excludes the decision threshold in either direction.
reframes.question: With a group-sequential test at tolerance 0.02 Brier on the paired difference from the 50-member baseline, after how many members per date does the question 'skill keeps rising past 50 members' resolve on the first 2 dates, measured on top-1% wind/temperature/rain Brier skill against ERA5?
reframes.measure: Run 2 dates in batches of 50 members up to 400 (at most 800 runs, roughly $110, about 8.5 machine-hours; expected $30-55 with early stopping), applying the sequential test after each batch.
reframes.compute_after: Compute becomes adaptive, spent only until the decision resolves; if 'no gain' resolves at 100-200 members, the remaining roughly $850 buys more dates or a perturbed-checkpoint diversity test instead of redundant members.
reframes.exact: Stopping member-count and the accepted hypothesis of the group-sequential test on the paired difference in top-1% fair-Brier skill between N members and the 50-member baseline.
reframes.expected: The test accepts 'no gain past 50' by 100-200 members per date, cutting member compute 5-10x relative to the 1,000-member plan.
reframes.fails_if: The true gain sits near the 0.02-Brier tolerance, so the test rarely stops early and costs about the same as the fixed design.
reframes.closest_prior: Group-sequential designs are standard in clinical trials; neither HENS [s_hens] nor the AIFS-ENS evaluation [s_crps_paper] used adaptive stopping, fixing member counts in advance.

glm.quote: reallocate a fixed number of member-forecasts across (dates x members) to minimize the standard error of the slope of skill vs log N, rather than maximizing members on few dates
glm.reason: Reallocates compute across dates vs members and measures slope standard error; compute then buys independent verification dates, new information, not redundant draws.

glm.quote: fit the score's a + b/N law from nested subsamples of a few hundred members and extrapolate the N-infinity asymptote directly, instead of buying the curve point by point with full-fidelity members
glm.reason: Changes what is measured: extrapolated N-infinity asymptote from an a + b/N fit; compute buys the asymptote and savings buy new dates/diversity.

glm.quote: a group-sequential test that adds members in batches of 50 and stops as soon as the confidence interval on the skill gain versus the 50-member baseline excludes the decision threshold in either direction
glm.reason: Reorders computation as adaptive sequential batches aimed at a binary decision; freed compute buys more dates or diversity, not redundant members.

reframes.bottleneck: The error floor lives in the fixed LOPLS-AA parameters, not in sampling. Once Green-Kubo noise is below the force-field bias (already true at 6x5 ns replicas), every added molecule or replica re-measures the same chemistry-dependent bias; time-parallel or longer sampling only shrinks noise that is not binding. Compute buys more of the same.
reframes.assumption: The force field must be taken as given: the ~25% floor is a fact to be documented, not a bias that compute can repair.
reframes.reframe: Change the unit of work from 'molecule at fixed force field' to 'force-field variant per molecule': derive per-molecule atomic charges from a cheap DFT single point (RESP-style) and rerun short Green-Kubo. If error drops, additional compute (more refit molecules, then class-specific LJ refits or delta-ML corrections) lowers the floor itself instead of documenting it.
reframes.question: On 12 molecules spanning C10-C50 and both hydrocarbon and ester chemistries, do per-molecule DFT/RESP charges cut held-out viscosity mean absolute percent error below 15% where stock LOPLS-AA charges give ~25%?
reframes.measure: Pick 12 molecules from the published set's high- and low-error ends (6 hydrocarbons, 6 esters). DFT single point plus RESP fit per molecule (~1 CPU-hour each, a few dollars), then 2x3 ns Green-Kubo per molecule at 40 C on one GPU, scoring viscosity error vs stock charges at identical sampling. Roughly $25-35 and a few days wall time.
reframes.compute_after: If the refit clears 15%, spend the full ~$950 on 120 charge refits plus an LJ correction fit, where each added dollar reduces error; if it partially works, escalate to class-specific LJ refits before any raw 120-molecule run.
reframes.exact: Per-molecule |eta_sim - eta_meas|/eta_meas at 40 C, averaged over the 12, stock vs refit charges at identical sampling; success = refit MAPE <= 15% and at least 10 percentage points below stock MAPE.
reframes.expected: Esters improve most, since their polarity is where generic charges err; MAPE falls from ~25% to ~12-18% and the viscosity bias sign shrinks or flips in at least 8 of 12 molecules.
reframes.fails_if: Refit MAPE stays >= 20% or improves by < 5 points: the floor then sits in LJ/dispersion or the transport model, not in charges, and per-molecule refits are not the lever.
reframes.closest_prior: Ogbomo 2026 ran stock LOPLS-AA only [s_ogbomo_md]; RESP charge derivation (Bayly 1993) is standard in OPLS/GAFF parameterization but was never varied in this benchmark [s_ogbomo_res].

reframes.bottleneck: The plan spends ~$940 mapping a floor it already hypothesizes, and defers the only test that could change the answer - whether a bias correction generalizes - to the largest, last set size. Steps are ordered biggest-spend-first.
reframes.assumption: A bias correction can only be fitted and validated once 120 molecules are in hand; the published 8 cannot support a correction model.
reframes.reframe: Invert the order of steps: fit a small chemistry-conditioned correction (chain length x ester/hydrocarbon, 2-4 parameters) on the already-published 8 molecules at zero MD cost, then buy the cheapest discriminating held-out set - 16 molecules at the corners of the correction axes - and scale only if the frozen correction generalizes. Additional molecules now buy correction generality, a different answer, rather than a finer map of the same floor.
reframes.question: Does a correction of at most 4 parameters fitted only on Ogbomo's 8 molecules hold on 16 held-out molecules, with held-out viscosity MAPE <= 15% and Spearman rank correlation >= 0.9 against measurement?
reframes.measure: Select 16 molecules at the extremes of chain length and chemistry from the 835-molecule set, run the existing protocol (6x5 ns, ~$4-5 per molecule at plan throughput, roughly $60-75 total), fit the correction on the published 8, freeze it, and score the 16. About one week.
reframes.compute_after: If it generalizes, the remaining 104 molecules (~$800) each tighten the correction and extend its domain, so compute changes predictions; if it fails, stop at ~$60 instead of $940.
reframes.exact: Held-out MAPE and Spearman rho on the 16 molecules using a correction fitted on 8 and frozen before scoring; success = MAPE <= 15% and rho >= 0.9; indeterminate band 15-20%.
reframes.expected: If the floor is a smooth function of chemistry as the hypothesis claims, held-out MAPE lands near 12-18% and rho near 0.8-0.95; thermal conductivity needs only a uniform down-shift since it is over-predicted for all 8 calibration molecules.
reframes.fails_if: Held-out MAPE >= 25% or rho <= 0.7 for every smooth correction family: the bias is not chemistry-smooth, no correction will generalize, and the 120-molecule run would only confirm the floor.
reframes.closest_prior: The bias signs and floor hypothesis come from the same 8-molecule study [s_ogbomo_res]; the closest prior calibration size is 8 [s_ogbomo_md] - this tests whether 8 was already enough.

reframes.bottleneck: What is measured - absolute viscosity and thermal conductivity at a single 40 C state point - is exactly where the force field is worst. Rank information is swamped by a chemistry-dependent offset that no amount of single-temperature sampling removes, so extra compute at 40 C cannot change the ranking.
reframes.assumption: The quantity that must rank correctly is the absolute 40 C transport value.
reframes.reframe: Change what is measured: rank candidates by their simulated temperature response (slope of log viscosity vs 1/T over 25-60 C, i.e., viscous activation energy, and the conductivity temperature ratio), where a multiplicative force-field error largely cancels. Compute spent at extra temperatures buys new discriminating signal instead of re-measuring a biased constant.
reframes.question: On the 8 published molecules, does the Spearman rank correlation between simulated and measured viscosity temperature-slope (d log eta / d(1/T) over 25-60 C) exceed 0.9, where absolute 40 C values sit below 0.7?
reframes.measure: Reuse the published protocol at 25 and 60 C on the same 8 molecules: 8 molecules x 2 temperatures x 6 replicas x 5 ns = 96 replicas, roughly $75 at plan throughput (halve replicas for ~$40). Regress log eta vs 1/T per molecule, compute Spearman rho of simulated vs measured slopes, and compare to the rho of 40 C absolutes.
reframes.compute_after: If slope ranking holds, the campaign becomes 3 temperatures x 40-120 molecules; every added molecule-temperature buys rank-relevant signal (roughly $2,800 for the full 120, or the same $950 over 40 molecules).
reframes.exact: Spearman rho between simulated and measured d(log eta)/d(1/T) across the 8 molecules, versus rho between simulated and measured eta at 40 C; success = slope-rho >= 0.9 and at least 0.2 above absolute-rho.
reframes.expected: If the dominant force-field error is a prefactor (consistent with a uniform over-prediction sign), simulated slopes rank 7-8 of 8 molecules correctly and slope-rho reaches 0.9+.
reframes.fails_if: Simulated slopes show rho <= 0.7 against measurement, or simulated activation energies are near-constant across molecules so there is no discriminating signal: the error is not a simple prefactor and the reframe is dead.
reframes.closest_prior: Ogbomo 2026 scored only single-temperature (40 C) absolutes on these molecules [s_ogbomo_md]; the reference set holds measured multi-temperature data that has not been used for scoring [s_ogbomo_db].

reframes.bottleneck: The compute axis scales molecule count (8→120) under one fixed force field, so if the error is a systematic LOPLS-AA bias, every added molecule buys the same biased estimate and the 25% floor cannot move — the plan itself labels compute 'not the lever' and then spends 59 machine-hours anyway.
reframes.assumption: The force field is held fixed: 'one fixed force field' (LAMMPS LOPLS-AA) appears in the hypothesis and test, and the chemistry-dependence of the error is asserted but never separated from the parameterization.
reframes.reframe: Swap the axes: fix a 16–24 molecule panel spanning hydrocarbons and esters, and spend the compute on a force-field/parameterization axis instead (2–3 off-the-shelf alternatives such as OPLS-AA and GAFF2, plus systematic LJ/torsion scaling of LOPLS). The measured quantity stays viscosity and thermal conductivity vs the same measured reference values, but each new run now tests a different error floor rather than re-sampling the same one.
reframes.question: On a fixed 24-molecule C10–C50 hydrocarbon/ester panel, does any of 6–8 classical force-field parameterizations bring held-out viscosity mean absolute percent error (measured against the reference set's experimental viscosities) below 15%, and what is each parameterization's signed thermal-conductivity error vs the measured conductivities?
reframes.measure: Re-run the published 8 molecules under two alternative off-the-shelf force fields with the identical 6×5 ns Green–Kubo protocol: 16 molecule-runs at the observed ~$4.50/molecule, roughly $70 and ~4.5 machine-hours, using the check-first machinery already built.
reframes.compute_after: Each additional dollar samples a new point in force-field space with a chance of breaking the 25% floor; compute now improves an error-vs-parameterization curve instead of adding molecules at a fixed floor, and any winning parameterization can then be scaled across molecules with the original plan.
reframes.exact: Viscosity MAPE < 15% and Spearman ρ vs measured viscosity > 0.9 on the 24-molecule panel for at least one parameterization, with per-class (hydrocarbon/ester) signed errors reported for both viscosity and thermal conductivity.
reframes.expected: One or two parameterizations cut hydrocarbon viscosity error to roughly 12–18% while esters stay above 20%, showing the floor is parameterization- and class-dependent rather than a universal chemistry constant; thermal-conductivity over-prediction persists across all of them.
reframes.fails_if: Every parameterization gives >25% viscosity error with the same sign pattern on the same molecules — then the floor is real for this class of fixed-charge force fields, and the molecule-scaling plan is certified as buying only more of the same.
reframes.closest_prior: Ogbomo 2026, eight molecules under a single force field [s_ogbomo_md]; this reframe keeps that protocol and adds the parameterization axis the block never varied.

reframes.bottleneck: Green–Kubo viscosity converges slowly (a collective stress autocorrelation), which is why each molecule costs 6×5 ns; most of the $940.98 buys statistical-noise reduction on an absolute quantity when the stated decision only needs a ranking of coolants.
reframes.assumption: That the quantity measured must be the Green–Kubo viscosity and thermal conductivity themselves, and that absolute accuracy against measurement must come before ranking can be trusted.
reframes.reframe: Change the measured quantity: compute self-diffusion coefficient D from mean-squared displacement, a single-particle average that converges roughly an order of magnitude faster than Green–Kubo stress integrals, and rank molecules by a diffusion–viscosity scaling relation (inverse D–η coupling / entropy scaling). Reserve expensive Green–Kubo for a small calibration subset that maps proxy to viscosity. A reverse-NEMD viscosity is a fallback proxy, also cheaper to converge than Green–Kubo.
reframes.question: On the published 8 molecules, does the Spearman rank correlation between 1/D (measured from 6×1 ns MSD trajectories) and the measured experimental viscosities match, within ±0.05, the Spearman correlation of the full 6×5 ns Green–Kubo viscosity against the same measured viscosities?
reframes.measure: Near-zero cost if the check-first trajectories are retained: re-analyze saved coordinates for MSD and D (~$0, analyst time only). If trajectories must be rerun: 8 molecules × 6 × 1 ns ≈ 48 ns, about one-fifth of the check-first run, roughly $10 and under 1 machine-hour.
reframes.compute_after: Each additional dollar screens roughly 5–10× more molecules for the ranking objective; Green–Kubo compute is spent only on a 12–16 molecule calibration/validation subset, so the 835-molecule reference set — not 120 — becomes the reachable screen size.
reframes.exact: Spearman ρ(proxy ranking, measured ranking) ≥ 0.9 on the 8 published molecules and on a held-out 16-molecule subset before any large proxy screen is committed; report ρ separately for hydrocarbons and esters.
reframes.expected: D-based ranking reaches ρ ≈ 0.85–0.95 for viscosity within the homologous series but fails for thermal conductivity, which needs its own calibration and remains on the expensive protocol.
reframes.fails_if: Proxy rank correlation < 0.8 on the 8-molecule check, or the D–η relation breaks at the hydrocarbon/ester class boundary (separate slopes per class) — then the proxy does not transfer and the original expensive protocol stands as the cheapest trustworthy ranker.
reframes.closest_prior: Ogbomo's 8-molecule Green–Kubo ranking against measurement [s_ogbomo_md]; the reference database [s_ogbomo_db] supplies the measured viscosities used to score the proxy.

reframes.bottleneck: The objective is raw per-molecule absolute error and rank correlation, so molecules are scored independently; yet the hypothesis claims the error is chemistry-dependent, i.e. structured and learnable. No pooling across chemistry classes is attempted, so more molecules buy only more uncorrected samples and the bias-correction threshold at 120 molecules is asserted, not measured.
reframes.assumption: The unit of work is one molecule scored alone, and bias correction is a pass/fail gate applied at the end rather than the object being estimated; the objective is taken to be absolute accuracy instead of the number of calibration molecules a shared correction needs.
reframes.reframe: Change the unit of work to a chemistry-class correction parameter and the objective to the learning curve of a class-conditional bias model (multiplicative correction per class with a chain-length slope). Compute buys calibration points at 8→16→24→48 molecules with held-out error measured at each size, and the decision question becomes how few molecules suffice to hold corrected error under threshold — a variant asks the same for a yes/no screen, refining replicas only for molecules near the decision threshold.
reframes.question: As the calibration subset grows 8→16→24→48 molecules, does leave-group-out viscosity MAPE after a two-class (hydrocarbon vs ester) multiplicative bias correction — measured per molecule as the MD-to-measured viscosity ratio against the reference set's experimental values — fall below 15% by 24 training molecules, and are the fitted correction factors stable to ±5% between subset sizes?
reframes.measure: First step costs ~$0: fit the two-class correction on the published 8 molecules' reported errors and leave-one-out cross-validate (analysis only). If LOO MAPE drops below ~20%, commission one 16-new-molecule tier (≈ $70, ~4.5 machine-hours) to confirm the curve direction before any 48- or 120-molecule spend.
reframes.compute_after: Each added molecule now shrinks a shared bias model for its whole class, so held-out error falls faster than 1/√N sampling; the 48- and 120-molecule tiers are spent only if the curve has not already flattened below 15%, and boundary-adaptive replica allocation buys classification confidence where it is cheapest.
reframes.exact: Stratified held-out viscosity MAPE < 15% at ≤24 training molecules with correction factors stable to ±5%; for the yes/no variant, ≥95% correct keep/reject calls at the coolant screening threshold with replicas concentrated within ±25% of the threshold viscosity.
reframes.expected: The hydrocarbon correction factor is constant within ±8%, cutting held-out error to ~12–18% by 16–24 molecules; esters need 24–48; the thermal-conductivity correction is the cleanest because the published bias was same-signed for all 8 molecules.
reframes.fails_if: Leave-one-out error on the 8-molecule fit stays ≥25%, or fitted correction factors vary by more than 50% across chain lengths within a class — then the 'chemistry-dependent floor' is per-molecule noise with no class structure, no pooled correction can beat it, and the original per-molecule scoring is the right unit after all.
reframes.closest_prior: The hypothesis [s_ogbomo_res] asserts the chemistry-dependent floor and the published 8-molecule comparison [s_ogbomo_md] supplies the first calibration set; no bias-model learning curve is measured anywhere in the block.

reframes.bottleneck: The text states the binding condition itself: batched simulation rollouts pay only if steering effects in simulation match the real robot, and for cloth that is false. So for exactly the tasks the field cares about (cloth, dish racks), every additional simulated rollout buys more of the same non-transferring number, and the 420k-rollout machinery pointed at deformables would produce confident answers about nothing real.
reframes.assumption: That the quantity to scale is absolute task success in simulation, and that sim-to-real mismatch is a property of the task rather than of the quantity being measured. A per-feature steering effect is a difference (steered minus baseline), and systematic simulator bias largely cancels inside a difference even when it corrupts absolute success.
reframes.reframe: Change what is measured: instead of scaling sim rollouts to estimate sim success rates, measure the transfer coefficient of the steering effect itself, i.e., whether the per-feature delta rank-orders the same in sim and on hardware. Compute then goes into many cheap paired comparisons across features rather than many episodes of an unvalidated proxy.
reframes.question: Is the per-feature steering effect (delta in task success vs unsteered baseline) rank-preserved between a GPU-parallel simulator and the real robot on one contact-rich task, measured as Spearman rho across at least 20 features with 25 paired episodes each?
reframes.measure: Pick plate-into-dish-rack insertion (contact-rich but rigid, has a real twin) and 20 features. Sim: 20 x 25 episodes batched over ~256 envs, roughly 50-100 GPU-hours (a few hundred dollars). Real: 20 x 25 episodes on one DROID cell, roughly 20-30 robot-hours over 1-2 weeks, a few thousand dollars. Cheapest screen first: recompute a coarse rho from already-published paired sim-vs-real steering numbers (e.g., COAST's LIBERO vs three real tasks), days of analysis at near-zero cost.
reframes.compute_after: If effect sizes transfer (rho clearly positive), the existing sweep infrastructure becomes meaningful for contact-rich tasks: scaling to hundreds of SAEs and hundreds of thousands of batched sim rollouts now predicts real-robot outcomes, which is exactly the unknown the problem cares about.
reframes.exact: For each of 20 features: sim delta = success_steered - success_base over 25 episodes in a ManiSkill twin of the task; real delta = same contrast over 25 episodes on the DROID setup; statistic = Spearman rho and per-feature sign agreement across the 20 (delta_sim, delta_real) pairs, with 95% bootstrap interval.
reframes.expected: Moderate positive transfer (rho roughly 0.4-0.7) for contact-rich rigid tasks, because the delta cancels fixed sim bias; likely weaker for cloth, which is itself a useful answer since it localizes where sim sweeps are trustworthy.
reframes.fails_if: rho is near zero or negative across features, meaning sim steering sweeps carry no signal about real contact-rich behaviour; then all further sim compute for cloth is wasted and the budget should move to real-robot episode collection.
reframes.closest_prior: The sweep of 520+ SAEs and 420k+ rollouts (arxiv 2603.19233), COAST conceptors reporting both sim (LIBERO 0.43 to 0.80) and real (+40% on three tasks) numbers for pi0.5, and RLinf-VLA's batched 256-environment ManiSkill rollouts (arxiv 2510.06710v2) as the sim-side engine.

reframes.bottleneck: The expensive unit is the closed-loop rollout: 300 sequential steps at ~150 ms each, 150 rollouts per feature across 135 features (20,250 episodes per answer). Most features are nulls, so the bulk of the compute buys confirmation of zeros; more GPUs only produce the same zeros faster.
reframes.assumption: That a feature's behavioural value can only be established by full closed-loop episodes, i.e., that no cheaper probe of the same feature predicts its closed-loop effect.
reframes.reframe: Change the order of steps and the unit of work: screen every feature with a batched open-loop probe (clamp or ablate the feature, measure the induced change in the action chunk on a fixed bank of recorded states, one forward pass per state instead of a 300-step episode), rank features by that probe, and buy closed-loop rollouts only for the top-k. The episode stops being the atomic unit.
reframes.question: Does the open-loop steering response, measured as mean L2 change in the action chunk over 1,000 recorded states per feature, rank the 135 features the same as their closed-loop delta-success ranking (Spearman rho between the two rankings, and recall of the true top-10 within the probe's top-30)?
reframes.measure: 135 features x 1,000 states = 135k steered forward passes, batched on one A100 in under 10 GPU-hours (tens of dollars), using states from the existing evaluation dataset; the closed-loop ground-truth ranking already exists from the published sweep, so the comparison itself is free.
reframes.compute_after: If the probe ranks well, each new sweep needs closed-loop rollouts for only ~top-10 features, cutting episodes per answer from ~20,250 to ~2,000; the same budget then sweeps roughly 10x more SAEs or tasks, which is what makes contact-rich and deformable coverage affordable.
reframes.exact: For each of the 135 features at its published steering strength: mean ||a_steered - a_base||_2 over the same 1,000 held-out states; Spearman rho of that 135-value ranking against published per-feature closed-loop delta-success (150 rollouts each); recall@30 of the closed-loop top-10.
reframes.expected: Moderate rank correlation (roughly 0.4-0.7) with high recall of every feature that has any closed-loop effect, since a feature that moves no action in 1,000 diverse states is unlikely to move behaviour in episodes; known risk from the VLA literature that open-loop metrics mis-rank closed-loop performance.
reframes.fails_if: rho below ~0.3 or any strongly closed-loop-effective feature falls outside the probe's top-30, meaning compounding closed-loop effects dominate single-step responses and screening must remain closed-loop.
reframes.closest_prior: The per-feature closed-loop sweep of 135 features x 150 rollouts in arxiv 2603.19233; the documented open-loop vs closed-loop evaluation gap for VLA policies is the standing evidence this might fail.

reframes.bottleneck: The headline unknown — whether any feature controls contact-rich or deformable behaviour — has only ever been tested with dictionaries fit on rigid pick-and-place and drawer activations. If the relevant directions are absent or dead in those SAEs, more rollouts over the same dictionary can only reproduce the same null, no matter how many GPUs are added. The SAE fit is cheap (a few GPU-hours); what is scarce is activations from the right distribution.
reframes.assumption: That features governing contact-rich and deformable behaviour exist in the model and are discoverable in activations collected from rigid tabletop rollouts, so the dictionary is not the limiting factor.
reframes.reframe: Change the objective's data: fit SAEs on activations from contact-rich and deformable episodes (scripted or teleoperated, failures included), then run the same ablation sweep. Compute shifts from rollouts-per-feature over a rigid dictionary to activation collection and dictionary fitting on the distribution where the answer is supposed to live.
reframes.question: Does an SAE fit on contact-rich activations contain at least one feature whose ablation changes contact-rich task success by 20 points or more, where a rigid-fit SAE of identical size shows a max effect of 5 points or less, measured as per-feature ablation delta-success over 25 episodes per feature?
reframes.measure: Collect ~500 contact-rich episodes (plate-in-rack plus cloth-grasp) in 256-environment batched ManiSkill (~1 GPU-day, ~150k activation steps); fit two SAEs with the published recipe (~6,700 Adam steps, a few GPU-hours each); ablate top-8 features per SAE x 25 episodes = 400 batched episodes (~1-2 GPU-days). Total roughly 100 GPU-hours, a few hundred dollars, no real robot required.
reframes.compute_after: If contact-fit SAEs expose causally effective features, the entire rollout-and-sweep apparatus finally has something to measure for cloth and dish racks, and scaling SAE counts and batched rollouts changes the answer instead of replicating a null; if neither dictionary shows any causal feature, that is strong evidence the VLA lacks steerable contact-rich internals and steering compute should stop in favor of data collection or pretraining.
reframes.exact: Two SAEs, same size and sparsity as arxiv 2603.19183, one fit on the contact-rich activation set and one on rigid-task activations; for each, ablate the top-8 features by activation frequency/variance; statistic = max over features of |success_ablated - success_base| on the contact-rich probe, 25 episodes per feature, compared between the two SAEs.
reframes.expected: At least one contact-fit feature with a clear causal effect (20+ points), by analogy with the rigid case where ablating four general features collapsed pi0.5 from 39/40 to 0/40; pi0.5 was trained on DROID-scale data containing contact-rich episodes, so the directions plausibly exist but were merged or dead in rigid-fit dictionaries.
reframes.fails_if: Max causal effect of the contact-fit SAE on the contact-rich probe is statistically indistinguishable from the rigid-fit SAE's and near zero, indicating the model has no internal knob for this behaviour class and further steering compute is futile.
reframes.closest_prior: The SAE recipe and cost model from arxiv 2603.19183, the rigid-task-only sweeps of arxiv 2603.19233, the pi0.5 ablation result (39/40 to 0/40) showing features can be strongly causal, and Grant et al.'s finding that motor programs are bound to recorded coordinates, i.e., that what gets stored depends on what data was seen.

reframes.bottleneck: Testing one feature costs 150 sequential closed-loop rollouts (up to 300 steps each, every step waiting on a ~150 ms forward pass plus the next observation), so answering whether any feature controls contact-rich or deformable behavior means months of serial robot or simulator time; an unbatched rollout also leaves the GPU idle while the simulator steps.
reframes.assumption: That a feature's effect can only be measured as closed-loop task success: the unit of measurement is a 300-step episode in which each observation causally depends on the previous action.
reframes.reframe: Change what is measured: score each feature by its open-loop action-chunk divergence (L2/KL between steered and unsteered predicted actions) on recorded contact-rich frames. Recorded observations break the step-after-step dependency, so every (frame, feature) pair is independent and thousands of steered forward passes batch on one GPU; serial closed-loop rollouts are reserved for the few features the screen promotes.
reframes.question: On the existing 135-feature rigid-task sweep, what is the Spearman rank correlation between per-feature open-loop action-chunk divergence (measured on ~10k recorded frames) and the already-measured closed-loop success delta per feature?
reframes.measure: Recompute each of the 135 steers as batched forward passes over ~10k recorded task frames (~1.35M forward passes, 1-3 A100-days batched, zero new rollouts), rank features by divergence, and correlate against the published 150-rollout success deltas; the episode logs already exist, so this is pure GPU inference plus an afternoon of statistics.
reframes.compute_after: If the screen validates (rho >= 0.7), the cloth question becomes embarrassingly parallel: sweep all 520 SAEs x all features against a few hours of recorded cloth and dish-rack teleoperation in GPU-weeks instead of robot-years, spending serial closed-loop rollouts only on the top-k; each added GPU buys a linear increase in features screened per day.
reframes.exact: Delta_i = mean over frames of ||a_steer_i - a_base||^2 on the action chunk (KL over action tokens as robustness check); Spearman rho with bootstrap CI between Delta_i and the closed-loop delta across the 135 features; prospective confirmation: top-5 open-loop features get 25 real rollouts each on one towel-fold task (125 episodes, ~2 robot-days).
reframes.expected: High correlation on rigid tasks: features that do nothing closed-loop should perturb nothing open-loop, and the large reported effects (+9 to +21 out of 25; 39/40 to 0/40) should produce large divergences; expect the screen to discard >80% of features at under 1% of the rollout cost.
reframes.fails_if: Open-loop divergence does not rank closed-loop success (rho < ~0.3), which existing VLA evaluations suggest is possible: small per-step action shifts can compound or be corrected under closed-loop feedback, in which case recorded-frame screening is worthless and the sequential rollout dependency is real.
reframes.closest_prior: Documented open-loop vs closed-loop gaps for VLAs (open-loop L2 predicting closed-loop success poorly in OpenVLA-class evaluations); RLinf-VLA's batched rollouts (1.61-1.88x with 256 ManiSkill envs) is the closed-loop alternative this would beat; action-token prediction accuracy is already used as a cheap proxy during VLA training.

reframes.bottleneck: The 20,250-episode answer was bought as 135 features x 150 rollouts at uniform precision; if most features are near-null, most episodes purchased no information, and the same waste scales to any future cloth sweep.
reframes.assumption: That the objective is a precise success estimate per feature (hence 150 trials for every feature), rather than a decision - is this feature worth testing on cloth, yes or no - or a ranking of the top few.
reframes.reframe: Change the objective from estimation to screening: run a sequential probability ratio test or successive halving over features, killing nulls after ~10 rollouts and concentrating budget near the decision boundary. Compute becomes an anytime resource that buys discrimination among top candidates instead of uniform confidence intervals over all 135.
reframes.question: Replaying the recorded outcomes of the completed 20,250 episodes: what fraction of the 135 features are correctly accepted or rejected at alpha=0.05 within <=20 rollouts under an SPRT, and does successive halving return the same top-10 features using <=30% of the episodes?
reframes.measure: Retrospective reanalysis only: implement SPRT (H0: delta=0 vs H1: |delta|>=0.2, alpha=beta=0.05) and successive halving on the logged per-episode success sequences, average over ~100 random episode orderings, and compare the selected feature set and episodes consumed against the full-data answer. Cost: hours of analyst time, no GPU, no robot.
reframes.compute_after: If the retrospective saving is >=3x, every future sweep inherits it: the same robot-week screens 3-10x more features, SAEs, or tasks, and the freed budget is what pays for the first contact-rich sweeps on real hardware.
reframes.exact: Per feature, replay episodes in shuffled order; record episodes-to-decision under SPRT and under successive halving with brackets at 10/30/90 rollouts; report median and 90th-percentile savings, false-accept/false-reject rates vs the full-data labels, and the rank correlation of the halving top-10 with the full-data top-10.
reframes.expected: Large savings: the reported effects are enormous (+9 to +21 out of 25, and 39/40 to 0/40 on ablation), so most decisions are statistically obvious within 10-20 episodes; expect >=70% episode reduction with an identical top-feature set.
reframes.fails_if: Most true effects are small (|delta| < 5 percentage points), so no early-stopping rule can separate them - but that itself would be the finding that steering effects are mostly negligible; also fails if outcomes drift over the sweep (non-i.i.d.), which inflates SPRT error rates and must be checked from the logs.
reframes.closest_prior: Wald's SPRT; Hyperband/ASHA and best-arm-identification bandits in hyperparameter search; adaptive-subsampling approaches in LLM evaluation (tinyBenchmarks, IRT-based efficient benchmarks) applying the same trick to expensive evals.

reframes.bottleneck: The one proven parallelization route - batched GPU sim rollouts, 1.61-1.88x at 256 ManiSkill environments - is written off because steering effects in simulation are assumed not to match the real robot ('false for cloth'), leaving all contact-rich steering evaluation serial on real hardware.
reframes.assumption: That steering-induced deltas inherit the full sim-to-real gap of the task: because absolute cloth behavior is wrong in sim, the effect of clamping a feature must also be wrong, so sim cannot even rank features for the real robot.
reframes.reframe: Test transfer of the delta, not the behavior. SAE features live in the network's activation space and encode its largely real-data-trained priors; the sim gap may sit in the physics while the feature-to-action-delta pathway is a property of the weights. If steering deltas correlate sim-to-real even when absolute success does not, sim becomes a valid screen and the parallel infrastructure applies directly.
reframes.question: Across >=12 features with known real-robot effects on a rigid tabletop task, is the Spearman correlation between sim-measured and real-measured steering success-deltas >=0.7, and what is that correlation on one deformable task (towel fold)?
reframes.measure: Build sim mirrors of 2-3 already-published steered tabletop tasks (~1 engineer-week), run batched sim rollouts for ~12 features x 100 episodes (1,200 episodes, 1-2 A100-days at 256 envs), reuse the published real numbers for rigid deltas, and add ~6 features x 25 real rollouts on one towel-fold task (~150 episodes, 2-3 days on one DROID-class setup). Total about 2 weeks.
reframes.compute_after: If rigid deltas transfer (rho >= 0.7) and cloth shows even rho ~ 0.5, the entire interpretability sweep moves to batched sim: compute then buys orders of magnitude - 420k-rollout-scale sweeps over all 520 SAEs and many deformable tasks become GPU-weeks, with real rollouts spent only confirming promoted features.
reframes.exact: Select features spanning the observed real effect range (+9, +15, +21 out of 25, plus the top-4 general features whose ablation took 39/40 to 0/40); replicate each steer in a ManiSkill/Isaac mirror of the DROID tabletop setup; delta_i = success(steer_i) - success(base) per domain; Spearman rho with bootstrap CI across features, reported separately for rigid and cloth.
reframes.expected: Rigid-task deltas plausibly transfer since those tasks succeed in both domains; cloth is the genuine bet - even a moderate positive correlation justifies sim pre-screening with real confirmation, still a 10-100x episode saving over pure real sweeps.
reframes.fails_if: Even rigid-task steering deltas fail to correlate (rho < 0.3), meaning the intervention pathway itself is sim-sensitive; then sim screening is dead at any physics fidelity and the remaining routes are open-loop screening or fixing cloth simulation first.
reframes.closest_prior: RLinf-VLA (256 parallel ManiSkill envs, 1.61-1.88x) as ready infrastructure; the deformable sim-to-real gap documented in cloth simulation benchmarks; analogous to RL findings that method or policy rankings can transfer sim-to-real even when absolute scores do not - treatment-effect rather than performance transfer.

glm.quote: Change the objective from estimation to screening: run a sequential probability ratio test or successive halving over features, killing nulls after ~10 rollouts and concentrating budget near the decision boundary.
glm.reason: Adaptive early stopping of closed-loop episodes; screening still uses closed-loop rollouts, never open-loop scoring on recorded observations.

reframes.bottleneck: Members are exchangeable draws of one afCRPS-trained distribution. Past ~50 members the Monte Carlo error of the tail probabilities is already small, so members 50->1,000 only re-measure the same shared, possibly biased tail distribution. More members buy more of the same.
reframes.assumption: That the only axis of ensemble growth is member count within one trained model, i.e. that tail sharpness is limited by sampling rather than by the single shared error of that one distribution.
reframes.reframe: Change the unit of work from members-per-model to sources-per-date: hold the pool at 200 members but build it from 4 partially independent sources (AIFS-ENS members from 4 staggered/lagged initial times valid at the same verification time, or checkpoint/seed variants), so compute buys error diversity instead of redraws.
reframes.question: At equal member count (200), does a 4-source mixed ensemble beat 200 exchangeable AIFS-ENS members on the 99th-percentile Brier score for 10 m wind, 2 m temperature, and 24 h rain over the 7 dates?
reframes.measure: Run 4 lagged initial times (-18 h, -12 h, -6 h, 0 h) x 50 members x 2 of the 7 dates = 400 forecasts (~$55 at ~$0.14/member). Pool into mixed 200-member sets and score against same-date 200-member pure AIFS-ENS subsamples, with block bootstrap over grid points.
reframes.compute_after: If mixed wins, scale to 7 dates x 4 sources x 250 members = 7,000 forecasts (~$960, same budget), then to 30 dates (~$4,000, 4x budget). True multi-seed retraining diversity is >$10k, but lagged/checkpoint diversity fits within ~1-4x budget.
reframes.exact: Variables: 10 m wind speed, 2 m temperature, 24-h accumulated precipitation. Threshold: ERA5 99th climatological percentile per grid point. Leads: days 3/7/10/15. Truth: ERA5. Scores: Brier of exceedance probability and fair CRPS. Comparison at equal N=200. Win criterion: mixed-ensemble Brier skill higher with 95% block-bootstrap CI excluding 0 on >=2 of 3 variables.
reframes.expected: Mixed ensemble wins on wind and rain at days 10-15, where model error dominates sampling error, and ties at day 3 where the single distribution is still sharp.
reframes.fails_if: Lagged/checkpoint member errors correlate >0.9 with the 0 h members, so pooling adds no diversity; then shared error is truly structural and only retraining or multi-model pooling helps, which exceeds the budget.
reframes.closest_prior: HENS Part 2: 7,424 single-model SFNO members [s_hens]; ECMWF lagged-ensemble practice and TIGGE multi-model results showing multi-source pools beat single-model ensembles at equal size.

reframes.bottleneck: Only 7 dates. Rare-extreme skill is dominated by which events happened to occur; refining probabilities on 7 fixed cases to 1,000 members buys precision on an answer that does not generalize. More compute buys more of the same 7 cases.
reframes.assumption: That the size-benefit measured on 7 dates transfers to extremes in general, i.e. that date-to-date variance is small relative to the 50-vs-1,000 member effect.
reframes.reframe: Change the unit of work from members-per-date to dates-at-moderate-N: spread the same total member budget as ~28 dates x 250 members, stratified toward dates with verified extreme events, and measure the distribution across events of the 50->250 member gain instead of one pooled number.
reframes.question: Across 28 dates, what fraction show a positive 50->250-member gain in top-percentile fair CRPS, and is the median per-date gain positive with a bootstrap CI excluding zero?
reframes.measure: Run 28 dates x 250 members = 7,000 forecasts (~$960, the existing budget), or a 14-date pilot = 3,500 members (~$480). Per date, subsample 50 vs 250 members, score top-percentile fair CRPS and Brier against ERA5, compute the per-date gain, then its sign distribution and median with 10,000 date-level bootstraps.
reframes.compute_after: If the median gain is positive but heterogeneous, scale to a 92-date season like HENS at 250 members = 23,000 forecasts (~$3,200, 3.2x budget); if gains concentrate in identifiable regimes, targeted date selection cuts this ~3x.
reframes.exact: Dates: 28 summer-2023 dates stratified so >=10 contain a verified ERA5 99th-percentile wind or rain event over domain land. Per-date gain = fairCRPS(50) - fairCRPS(250) at the top-percentile threshold, same truth and thresholds as the plan. Report median, IQR, fraction positive, and 95% bootstrap CI. Decision: median gain CI excludes 0.
reframes.expected: Median per-date gain near zero with large spread: a few long-lead wind/rain event dates show real gains, most dates are flat, implying saturation holds on average but not per-event.
reframes.fails_if: Per-date scoring noise at 250 members exceeds the gain signal (median CI spans zero at 28 dates); then no feasible date count within ~4x budget resolves the question and the project needs an archived multi-season reforecast instead of new runs.
reframes.closest_prior: HENS Part 2 evaluated 92 summer-2023 dates [s_hens]; the AIFS-ENS evaluation in [s_crps_paper] uses seasonal samples rather than 7 cases.

reframes.bottleneck: The plan spends the whole budget tracing score vs N whose endpoint (the N→∞ asymptote = the single-distribution ceiling) can be estimated first, cheaply. If the distribution is under-dispersive in the tail, no member count helps and the spend is wasted.
reframes.assumption: That the ceiling must be discovered by running 1,000 members, i.e. that the steps cannot be reordered to estimate the asymptote and dispersion before paying for the full curve.
reframes.reframe: Change the order of steps: fit score(N) = a + b/N from a small pilot to estimate the N→∞ asymptote, and measure tail dispersion via rank histograms conditioned on verified 99th-percentile outcomes, before any large run. Proceed to 1,000 members only if the asymptote beats the 50-member score by a pre-set margin; otherwise redirect the budget to a recalibration/spread-inflation sweep, which is nearly free once members exist.
reframes.question: From N = 25, 50, 100, 200 members on 2 dates, is the fitted N→∞ asymptote of top-percentile fair CRPS more than 2% better than the 50-member score, and is the ensemble under-dispersive conditional on ERA5 99th-percentile exceedances?
reframes.measure: 2 dates x 200 members = 400 forecasts (~$55, <6% of budget). Fit per-grid-point top-percentile fair CRPS linearly in 1/N with bootstrap CI on the asymptote; compute tail-conditional rank histograms and spread/error ratio. This gates the remaining ~$900.
reframes.compute_after: If the asymptote is promising, run the planned 7 x 1,000 (~$960). If capped and under-dispersive, redirect to a recalibration sweep: ~8 spread-inflation factors applied in post-processing to 50 members x 7 dates (base runs ~$48, scoring negligible) plus 250 members on winning settings (~$240), total under $350, leaving budget for the diversity or date-spread reframes.
reframes.exact: Pilot: 2 of the 7 dates, each with at least one verified 99th-percentile wind and rain event. N in {25,50,100,200}. Regress top-percentile fair CRPS on 1/N, report asymptote a with 95% CI. Under-dispersion flag: upper-tail rank-histogram excess and spread/error ratio < 0.8 conditional on ERA5 exceedances. Go criterion: (a - score(50))/score(50) < -2% with CI excluding 0.
reframes.expected: Small b/N slope: asymptote within ~1% of the 50-member score for wind and rain at days 10-15 (saturation), plus mild tail under-dispersion, so the gate redirects spend to recalibration, matching the 'shared error caps skill' branch.
reframes.fails_if: The 2-date pilot's asymptote CI cannot exclude either branch; but then 7 dates x 1,000 members cannot resolve the question either (same dates, more N only shrinks sampling error), so the gate still wins by exposing this for $55 instead of $963.
reframes.closest_prior: Standard 1/N Monte Carlo convergence of fair-CRPS/Brier ensemble-size subsampling as in [s_crps_paper]; HENS [s_hens] showed gains persisting to 7,424 members for SFNO, a different and likely more dispersive model.

reframes.bottleneck: The 1,000-member forecasts only reduce Monte-Carlo noise in the probability estimates of one learned distribution. If members really are exchangeable draws, the fair-CRPS/Brier gain from 50 to 1,000 members is fixed by sampling theory, so roughly $900 of the $963 buys a number predictable from ~200 members.
reframes.assumption: That the skill-versus-members curve must be measured with real 1,000-member forecasts, i.e., that members beyond ~50 carry new information rather than re-sampling the same afCRPS-trained distribution.
reframes.reframe: Reorder the steps: measure exchangeability first. Estimate pairwise member error correlation and effective ensemble size N_eff from a small pilot, derive the sampling-theory bound on the 50-to-1,000 skill gain, and validate the subsampling methodology for free on the existing 7,424-member HENS archive. Only run 1,000 members if measured correlation makes N_eff much smaller than N.
reframes.question: At leads of 1, 5 and 10 days, what is the mean pairwise error correlation rho among AIFS-ENS v1 members for 10 m wind, 2 m temperature and rain, and is the fair-CRPS gain predicted for 50 to 1,000 members, using N_eff = N/(1+(N-1)rho), larger than 1%?
reframes.measure: Run 100 members x 2 dates (~200 member-forecasts at ~$0.11 each, about $22, near the $19.90 check-first gate), compute pairwise member RMSE correlations per field and lead, derive N_eff and the beta-binomial sampling bound on Brier improvement; cross-check the skill-curve shape by subsampling the free HENS 7,424-member x 92-date archive on CPU.
reframes.compute_after: If members are near-iid, the 50-vs-1,000 question is settled for ~$25 and the remaining ~$900 buys more verifying dates, which is the real binding constraint on top-percentile skill confidence intervals. If rho is large, compute now buys diagnosis of a correlated-error structure the original design cannot even see.
reframes.exact: Mean pairwise member RMSE correlation rho for 10 m wind at day 5 across 100 members x 2 dates; N_eff(N) = N/(1+(N-1)rho); predicted Brier(1,000) minus Brier(50) from beta-binomial sampling of the event probabilities.
reframes.expected: rho small but positive (0.05-0.3); predicted 50-to-1,000 skill gain under 1-2%, i.e., saturation is largely a sampling identity, decided an order of magnitude cheaper than planned.
reframes.fails_if: A 200-vs-50-member subsample already beats the iid sampling bound, implying non-exchangeable structure (member drift or sub-populations) that only full 1,000-member runs can characterize.
reframes.closest_prior: HENS Part 2's 7,424-member tail sampling [s_hens]; the afCRPS paper's exchangeable-draws training claim [s_crps_paper]; classical effective-ensemble-size analysis (Leutbecher & Palmer 2008).

reframes.bottleneck: Estimating top-percentile probabilities by counting members makes cost scale linearly with tail rarity: the 99th percentile needs ~100 members, the 99.9th ~1,000, and each extra nine of rarity costs 10x the GPUs to sample the same unchanged distribution.
reframes.assumption: That the ensemble tail must be sampled empirically; that no cheaper estimator can extract more tail information per member.
reframes.reframe: Change the unit of work from member count to member-plus-tail-model: fit a generalized Pareto tail (peaks over threshold) to each grid point's 50-member ensemble and compare its exceedance probabilities against empirical counts from 200-1,000 members. If 50 fitted members match 1,000 raw members, member count stops being the compute axis.
reframes.question: Do GPD tails fitted to 50-member AIFS-ENS ensembles reproduce the top-1% exceedance-probability fields of a 1,000-member ensemble within the 1,000-member bootstrap sampling error, for 10 m wind, 2 m temperature and daily rain at days 5-10?
reframes.measure: Free methodology check on the existing HENS 7,424-member x 92-date archive: fit GPD to 50-member subsamples and score against the 7,424-member empirical tails (CPU-hours, under $5). Then one AIFS confirmation: 200 members x 1 date, about $22.
reframes.compute_after: If the tail model holds, every 50-member forecast yields 1,000-member-grade tail probabilities, so the same $963 buys roughly 20x more dates or variables, i.e., more independent extreme events to verify against, which is what actually limits rare-extreme skill estimates.
reframes.exact: Mean absolute error between 50-member GPD-fitted and 1,000-member empirical 99th-percentile exceedance probabilities over land grid points, compared against the 95% bootstrap band of the 1,000-member empirical estimate.
reframes.expected: Fitted tails within sampling noise at the 99th percentile, degrading near the 99.9th where even 1,000 members leave at most ~10 tail samples per grid point.
reframes.fails_if: The afCRPS-trained ensemble has bounded or light (shape xi < 0) tails, so GPD extrapolation biases exceedance probabilities beyond the fitted range and raw member count is genuinely the only route to rarer tails.
reframes.closest_prior: HENS Part 2's 4-sigma claims from raw 7,424-member counts [s_hens]; standard peaks-over-threshold/GPD extreme-value practice (Coles 2001); EVT-style tail extension behind products like ECMWF's EFI.

reframes.bottleneck: The hypothesized cap is error shared by all members, yet the design varies only member count within one trained distribution: it can detect a plateau but cannot spend its way past it, so at saturation each extra GPU-hour provably buys more of the same.
reframes.assumption: That the single AIFS-ENS v1 weight set must be held fixed; that an ensemble means draws of one distribution rather than a choice of how many distinct error modes to sample per dollar.
reframes.reframe: Hold GPU-hours fixed and make diversity the axis: K error-decorrelated ensembles (different training checkpoints or seeds of the afCRPS run, or AIFS-ENS pooled with another ML ensemble) with N/K members each, versus N members of the single model. Score top-percentile Brier and fair CRPS at equal cost.
reframes.question: At equal GPU-hours, does pooling 5 training checkpoints x 200 members beat 1,000 members of the single AIFS-ENS v1 distribution on top-1% 10 m-wind Brier score, i.e., does between-checkpoint error decorrelation exceed the within-ensemble sampling gain?
reframes.measure: Pilot: 3 checkpoints x 100 members x 1 date (~300 member-forecasts, about $33; checkpoints already exist from training, inference only). Measure the top-1% wind Brier of the pooled 300-member ensemble versus 300 members of the reference checkpoint, plus the between-checkpoint day-5 RMSE correlation as the diversity diagnostic.
reframes.compute_after: If diversity wins, more compute buys additional independent error modes, so skill can keep rising exactly where the single-model curve was flat, and the design directly tests the root question's shared-error cap instead of only observing a plateau. If pooling 3 checkpoints gains nothing, the shared-error cap is confirmed early and cheaply.
reframes.exact: Difference in top-1% 10 m-wind Brier score between (a) 300 members pooled across 3 checkpoints and (b) 300 members of the reference checkpoint on one shared date, with between-checkpoint 10 m-wind error correlation at days 1, 5 and 10.
reframes.expected: Checkpoints from one training run show high day-5 error correlation and pooling gains little, confirming shared error dominates; any measurable decorrelation reopens the skill curve at fixed budget.
reframes.fails_if: Only one usable checkpoint exists, or between-checkpoint error correlation exceeds 0.99 at all leads, so the diversity axis buys nothing and the single-distribution design stands.
reframes.closest_prior: Multi-model versus single-model ensemble comparisons showing diversity beats size at fixed cost (TIGGE/ENSEMBLES-era results; Leutbecher & Palmer 2008); HENS [s_hens] as the single-model large-N reference point.

reframes.bottleneck: Almost the whole budget repeats one estimator, Green-Kubo on six 5-ns replicas. For heavy C30-C50 liquids the stress autocorrelation decays slowly, so 5 ns truncates its tail and the observed ~25% 'floor' confounds force-field bias with estimator truncation and sampling noise; more identical replicas only shrink variance as 1/sqrt(N) around a possibly truncated integral.
reframes.assumption: The 25% deviation from measurement is a pure force-field error, independent of how viscosity is extracted from the trajectory and independent of run length.
reframes.reframe: Change what is measured: compute viscosity by reverse non-equilibrium MD (Muller-Plathe momentum exchange) on the same force field and boxes, which for viscous liquids converges with far less sampling than Green-Kubo, and compare both estimators against measurement on the heaviest published molecules.
reframes.question: For the two most viscous molecules in the published eight, does rNEMD with standard error under 3% shift the deviation from the measured viscosity by more than 5 percentage points relative to the Green-Kubo value?
reframes.measure: Run rNEMD on the two heaviest published molecules, 3 independent runs each, plus one control GK replica; about 20 replica-equivalents, roughly $25-30 (under 5% of budget).
reframes.compute_after: If the estimator moves the deviation, per-molecule cost on heavy molecules drops and bias attribution changes; the 120-molecule scan is recosted with the better estimator and compute buys coverage toward the 835-molecule set instead of repeated GK noise.
reframes.exact: Report per molecule: GK viscosity from 6x5 ns, rNEMD viscosity with SE from 3 runs, and the measured value; the reframe passes if |rNEMD - measured| differs from |GK - measured| by more than 5 percentage points on either heavy molecule.
reframes.expected: GK under-converges for the heaviest molecules (tail truncated at 5 ns), so rNEMD shifts their values by 5-15%, showing part of the floor is estimator, not force field.
reframes.fails_if: rNEMD and GK agree within 3% and both sit ~25% off measurement; then the floor really is the force field, no estimator change helps, and spend should move to force-field correction rather than sampling.
reframes.closest_prior: Muller-Plathe 1997 reverse-NEMD, validated on alkanes and known to outperform Green-Kubo for viscous fluids; [s_ogbomo_md] used Green-Kubo only.

reframes.bottleneck: Pass/fail is set on held-out absolute error, but the downstream task is ranking coolants. If the force field's error is shared across chemically similar molecules it cancels in pairwise comparisons, so the plan could declare 'not the lever' while the ranking it feeds is already fine, or the reverse; more molecules under the current objective only buy tighter estimates of an absolute error that may not cap ranking.
reframes.assumption: A ~25% absolute error floor caps rank correlation; the hypothesis treats the error floor and the ranking cap as the same thing.
reframes.reframe: Change the objective: score pairwise ordering accuracy and Spearman rank of computed versus measured properties first, with absolute error as a secondary diagnostic, and test whether ordering is already good at n=8.
reframes.question: On the published eight molecules, what fraction of the 28 viscosity pairs and 28 thermal-conductivity pairs are ordered correctly, and is Spearman rho >= 0.9 for either property?
reframes.measure: Pure reanalysis of the published eight-molecule table [s_ogbomo_md] with bootstrap resampling over molecules; no new simulation, roughly $0 in compute.
reframes.compute_after: If pairwise ordering is already >=0.9, each additional molecule adds O(n) pair tests, so compute directly sharpens rank confidence and the 120-molecule run becomes the decisive ranking measurement; if ordering is poor, ranking is truly capped and compute should fund force-field improvement instead of more molecules.
reframes.exact: Compute pairwise ordering accuracy and Spearman/Kendall rank correlation of MD versus measured viscosity and thermal conductivity for the eight molecules, with bootstrap confidence intervals over resampled molecules.
reframes.expected: Viscosity ordering is strong (rho near 0.9) despite ~25% absolute error because the error is monotonic in chain length; thermal conductivity ordering is weaker.
reframes.fails_if: Pairwise ordering accuracy is below ~0.8 at n=8, or bootstrap intervals are too wide to decide; then ranking is capped by chemistry-dependent scatter and more molecules under this force field only confirm the cap.
reframes.closest_prior: [s_ogbomo_md] itself; the reordering analysis needs no data beyond its eight-molecule comparison.

reframes.bottleneck: The unit of work is fixed at 5-ns sequential replicas, so wall-clock per molecule is set by the longest chain, and no one has measured whether 5 ns is wastefully long for light molecules or fatally short for heavy ones; replicas already run side by side, so no new parallel scheme wins, but the unit size itself is unmeasured. More compute spent in 5-ns units buys only more of the same unit.
reframes.assumption: 5 ns is the right replica length for every C10-C50 molecule, and replicas must be that long because decorrelation is slow.
reframes.reframe: Change the unit of work and the order of steps: first measure the forgetfulness of the sampling chain - the stress-autocorrelation decay time and the Green-Kubo running-integral plateau for the heaviest molecule - then size replicas to a few decorrelation times; if that is far below 5 ns, replace 6 long replicas with many short decorrelated-started replicas run side by side, cutting wall-clock per molecule.
reframes.question: For the heaviest published molecule at 40 C, at what time does the normalized stress autocorrelation fall below 0.05, and does the Green-Kubo running viscosity integral plateau (change under 5% over its last half) before 5 ns?
reframes.measure: Append one 20-ns run of the heaviest molecule to the check-first replicate (about 4 replica-equivalents, roughly $5-10) and block-analyze the autocorrelation and running integral; no new setup needed.
reframes.compute_after: If the plateau comes well before 5 ns, replicas shrink and multiply: the same budget buys 5-10x more molecules or replicas with perfect side-by-side parallelism, making compute the lever for coverage of the 835-molecule set. If the integral still rises at 5 ns, the current unit underestimates heavy-molecule viscosity, longer runs are mandatory, and the ladder must trade molecule count for run length.
reframes.exact: From the 20-ns trajectory report: the SACF normalized to its t=0 value versus time; the time it falls below 0.05; the GK running integral at 1, 2, 5, 10 and 20 ns; and the fractional change between 5 ns and the plateau.
reframes.expected: For C50-sized molecules the SACF tail runs to several ns and the 5-ns integral misses 10-20% of the viscosity, while C10 plateaus under 1 ns; one replica length is wrong at both ends.
reframes.fails_if: The running integral is still rising at 20 ns for the heaviest molecules; then viscosity at 40 C needs runs too long to parallelize away, and the honest fix is the estimator change above or accepting a heavy-molecule bias.
reframes.closest_prior: Standard Green-Kubo convergence studies showing slow stress-autocorrelation tails for long-chain alkanes; the plan's own check-first replicate of [s_ogbomo_md] provides the launch point.

reframes.bottleneck: The hypothesized ~25% chemistry-dependent error floor is a systematic force-field bias: more molecules, more replicas, or longer trajectories only re-measure the same bias at higher precision, so compute past ~48 molecules buys more of the same.
reframes.assumption: The quantity scored against measurement must be each molecule's absolute viscosity and thermal conductivity.
reframes.reframe: Change the measured quantity from absolute properties to paired differences: compute Δη and Δλ between molecule pairs with an identical protocol, where shared systematic error partially cancels, and score sign agreement against measured differences. Compute then buys correct ordering decisions rather than absolute accuracy.
reframes.question: For molecule pairs whose measured viscosities differ by at least 15%, what fraction have sign(Δη_simulated) = sign(Δη_measured) when both legs use the same LOPLS-AA Green-Kubo protocol?
reframes.measure: 20 molecule pairs spanning 1–50 mPa·s from the reference set, 2 replicas × 5 ns per leg (200 ns total), count sign agreement of simulated vs measured viscosity differences. Rough cost $35 (about 2 machine-hours at the plan's throughput), done before scaling further.
reframes.compute_after: More compute adds pairs and resolves near-tie pairs with extra replicas, directly improving decision accuracy at ranking boundaries instead of re-measuring a fixed bias.
reframes.exact: Sign agreement = fraction of the 20 pairs where the simulated viscosity difference has the same sign as the measured difference, with per-leg η from the standard Green-Kubo integral at 40 °C.
reframes.expected: Sign agreement ≥ 0.85 for pairs separated by ≥15% measured difference, even while absolute per-molecule error remains ~25%, showing the floor is largely common-mode.
reframes.fails_if: Sign agreement ≤ 0.6 on well-separated pairs, meaning the error is molecule-specific noise rather than shared systematic bias, so differencing buys nothing.
reframes.closest_prior: Ogbomo's 8-molecule study compared absolute simulated vs measured values only [s_ogbomo_md]; no paired-difference error cancellation has been tested on this set [s_ogbomo_db].

reframes.bottleneck: Green-Kubo viscosity and thermal conductivity converge slowly, so most of the $940 budget buys statistical averaging of a quantity whose accuracy is capped by the force field; the unit of work (30 ns of transport-coefficient sampling per molecule) is the most expensive way to obtain a ranking signal.
reframes.assumption: The screening quantity must be the transport coefficient itself, estimated by Green-Kubo.
reframes.reframe: Change the unit of work: screen with self-diffusion from the Einstein relation (converges roughly an order of magnitude faster than Green-Kubo viscosity) plus density, and reserve expensive Green-Kubo runs for survivors of a funnel over all 835 molecules — but only after checking the proxy actually tracks measured viscosity.
reframes.question: Across 40 molecules spanning the reference set's chemistry classes, does the Spearman rank correlation between simulated self-diffusion coefficient and measured viscosity exceed |ρ| = 0.8?
reframes.measure: 40 molecules, one 2-ns replica each for mean-squared-displacement slope and density (80 ns total), compute Spearman ρ between D_sim and measured η at 40 °C. Rough cost $15, under one machine-hour.
reframes.compute_after: If the proxy holds, each additional dollar buys funnel depth — cheap D screening on hundreds of molecules, Green-Kubo only on the top slice — so compute changes which candidates advance rather than polishing a capped estimate.
reframes.exact: Spearman ρ between D_sim (Einstein MSD slope, 40 °C, LOPLS-AA) and measured η across the 40 molecules, with a per-class breakdown for alkanes vs esters.
reframes.expected: |ρ| ≥ 0.8 overall and ≥ 0.7 within the ester class, sufficient to justify a two-stage screen where Green-Kubo is spent on ≤ 20% of candidates.
reframes.fails_if: |ρ| < 0.5 overall or within any major class, meaning diffusion is not an informative proxy for viscosity here and the funnel would misdirect the expensive runs.
reframes.closest_prior: Ogbomo ran Green-Kubo only on 8 molecules [s_ogbomo_md]; the 835-molecule reference set has no validated cheap-proxy screening stage [s_ogbomo_db].

reframes.bottleneck: The objective is global rank agreement over the whole benchmark, and the force field is held fixed; that combination guarantees the error floor caps the metric no matter how many molecules are added, and the plan's scalar bias correction is applied after the fact rather than learned.
reframes.assumption: The force field must stay fixed, and success means a single global rank correlation across all benchmark molecules.
reframes.reframe: Change the objective to a yes/no decision — is candidate X better than the incumbent coolant on both η and λ? — and unfix the field minimally by learning a class-conditional correction (per chemistry class, linear in carbon number) jointly with the benchmark, with compute allocated adaptively to molecules nearest the decision boundary.
reframes.question: Can a class-conditional linear correction fit on 30 molecules with known measurements reduce held-out viscosity error below 15% and raise better/worse-than-incumbent decision accuracy above 90% on 20 held-out molecules?
reframes.measure: Run 22 new molecules (reusing the published 8 for the fit set) at 6 replicas × 5 ns (~660 ns), fit per-class slope/intercept corrections on 30, evaluate held-out MAPE and decision accuracy on 20. Rough cost $110 (about 7 machine-hours).
reframes.compute_after: Further compute buys boundary resolution: extra replicas and extra molecules are spent only where the classification is uncertain, so more compute moves candidates across the decision line instead of shrinking error bars on a capped global rank.
reframes.exact: Held-out viscosity MAPE after applying the class-conditional correction, and decision accuracy = fraction of 20 held-out molecules correctly classified as better or worse than the incumbent on both η and λ.
reframes.expected: Held-out error < 15% and decision accuracy ≥ 0.9 with the correction explaining most of the chemistry-dependent bias (correction R² > 0.7).
reframes.fails_if: Residual held-out error stays above 25% with correction R² < 0.3, i.e., no class structure to the bias, meaning the error is irreducible per-molecule noise and neither correction nor boundary-focused compute can help.
reframes.closest_prior: The plan's own bias-correction step treats error as a single scalar [s_ogbomo_res]; no class-conditional or decision-threshold framing appears in [s_ogbomo_md] or [s_ogbomo_db].

Compute then buys correct ordering decisions rather than absolute accuracy.
